title: Agentic AI Chat
description: An AI agent embedded in LinkedIn's observability tools, now used by 10,000+ engineers to find an incident's root cause faster.
blurb: Embedded with product engineers, I led end-to-end UX for a conversational AI agent now used across observability tools by 10,000+ LinkedIn engineers. I set the UX principles for LLM-powered interactions, spec'd the contextual input, plugins, and inline-artifact components the team builds on, and designed a custom icon system that signals a trusted, purpose-built tool. The result is faster incident triage and lower cognitive load for engineers working mid-incident.

hero.alt: Observe Agent chat home screen, embedded in the observability product
hero.caption: The empty state had three getting-started prompts, not a blank box waiting for input.

blocks.value: Observe Agent is a conversational AI surface built into LinkedIn's observability tools: alerts, metrics, logs, and deployment history. I led end-to-end UX for the experience alongside the product engineers building it: the interaction model, the plugin and inline-artifact components other designers now build on, and the visual identity that signals a trustworthy, purpose-built tool rather than a generic bot.
It ships to 10,000+ engineers and has cut the time it takes them to trace an incident (a service disruption, a spike in latency) back to its root cause.

The people using this are Site Reliability Engineers and on-call engineers, almost always mid-incident: several tabs open across alerting, metrics, logs, and deployment history, under real time pressure. Before designing anything, I wrote down what that person actually needed from the agent, to align the team on the job to be done, not on what would be a fun AI feature to add.

blocks.alt: User-needs statements from a Site Reliability Engineer persona, framed as "I want to…" jobs
blocks.caption: The persona stated as jobs to do, not a bio: diagnose, drill into evidence, revisit later.

blocks.value: That's the common thread: high-pressure, multi-tab work, split across tooling that doesn't talk to each other. Every decision after this had to earn its place against that reality.

sections.heading: The Agent Lives Beside the Data

blocks.value: The agent had to feel native to the product, not bolted onto it: sitting beside the same logs and metrics views engineers already use, and not just reading context from them. Ask it to show errors during lunch, and it sets the filters in the view itself, rather than telling the engineer where to click or sending them off to a separate destination to do it themselves.

blocks.alt: The agent conversation shown alongside a logs explorer view, having just applied filters to that view on the engineer's behalf
blocks.caption: It didn't just answer: it applied the filters itself in the Logs Explorer.

sections.heading: A Side Panel, Sized to the Task

blocks.value: Where the agent lived on screen was its own decision, not a default. I audited how side panels already behaved elsewhere in the product, full takeovers, modals, docked panels, and built a storyboard to argue the case: a **persistent side panel** that keeps the underlying page in view, narrow when it's supplying supplementary information, wider once the interaction turns into something closer to create-and-edit. A modal or a full-screen takeover would have solved for the chat and lost the page it's supposed to be chatting about.

blocks.alt: Storyboard of side-panel placement options, showing how the chat panel shares screen space with the existing application
blocks.caption: The audit that argued for a side panel over a takeover, narrow or wide depending on the task.

sections.heading: Three Primitives: Plugins, Context, and Inline Artifacts

blocks.value: Underneath the chat itself, I spec'd three components everything else builds on: **plugins** for the agent's tools and skills, **contextual input** for pulling a page element, a chart, a job, an alert, into the conversation as a removable tag, and **inline artifacts** so a chart renders directly in the chat instead of linking out to it. That last one was the real tradeoff: it would have been simpler to answer in text and link to the real dashboard, but that hands the engineer another tab to lose their place in. Rendering the answer where the question was asked cost more design and engineering effort up front, and was worth it.

blocks.alt: Interaction specs for chat input, plugins menu, contextual tags, and inline chart artifacts
blocks.caption: Plugins, tags, and inline charts, spec'd once so the whole team builds the same grammar.

blocks.value: A generic bot icon would have undercut the one thing this needed to earn: trust from someone deciding whether to act on what the agent just told them mid-incident. I ran a comparison audit of the sparkle and bot iconography already in use elsewhere, then designed a mark that pairs a sparkle (AI) with the shape of a telescope (Observe), built out in variations for every channel it appears in, the product UI and Slack. That exploration reached further than the icon: an early concept named the Slack bot separately, O11y Copilot, before the team settled on one name, Observe Agent, everywhere it appears, so the identity stayed consistent in name as well as mark.

blocks.alt: Icon design work: a comparison audit of sparkle glyphs and the final telescope-plus-sparkle mark in its variations
blocks.caption: An early concept split the name: O11y Copilot in Slack, before the team settled on one.

blocks.value: The classic UX toolkit didn't disappear designing this, it just changed shape. Personas became short need statements instead of a persona board, a storyboard audited screen real estate instead of a user flow, and the artifact the rest of the team actually built from wasn't a wireframe, it was the interaction spec for the plugin and inline-artifact primitives.

What I'd revisit: the panel model assumes one conversation, one side panel, at a time. It hasn't been tested against an engineer running two or three investigations in parallel, which is closer to how a bad incident actually goes. I'd want real usage data before deciding whether the component set needs a second surface, not just a wider one.

title: Genomic Data Platform
description: A customer described, on a support call, exactly the comparison tool bioinformaticians needed. It shipped, and became how scientists spot which genes vary across patient cohorts.
blurb: As Senior Staff Interaction Designer, I led UX across Illumina's Connected Analytics platform for multiomic analysis, spanning genomics, proteomics, and spatial transcriptomics apps built on a shared design system, data model, and user base. I grounded the work in evidence-based personas, card sorting with bioinformaticians, and ongoing field research, then turned direct customer feedback into shipped visualization features. The result is a cohesive platform that helps scientists compare groups of subjects and accelerate biomarker and drug discovery.
team: UX researchers, bioinformatics subject-matter experts, product stakeholders

hero.alt: The Cohorts survival-comparison view: a Kaplan–Meier curve comparing four subject groups with a p-value confidence matrix
hero.caption: A p-value matrix sits beside the curves: how cohorts diverge, and how confident to be.

blocks.value: Cohorts, by Illumina Connected Analytics, lets customers aggregate and analyze genomic and clinical data using private, public, and partner data sets, then compare groups of subjects to **accelerate biomarker and drug discovery**.

Interviews with stakeholders and subject matter experts surfaced three roles: the research scientist, the bioinformatician, and the developer or admin who provisions access. I **designed for one of them**. The research scientist chasing a biomarker was the persona everything else served, and the pain point that shaped the most decisions was a simple one: “My research often gets bogged down because I can't easily find enough data.”

blocks.alt: Personas for the genomics scientist, bioinformatician, and developer/admin, with goals and a pain-point quote
blocks.caption: Design decisions served one of three roles: the scientist chasing a biomarker.

blocks.value: I ran card sorting sessions with subject matter experts to settle the **shared vocabulary** underneath that persona's work, from panel design through sequencing and secondary analysis to case interpretation. Getting that terminology right mattered more than it sounds: it's the language every screen in the platform would eventually use.

blocks.alt: A remote card sorting session grouping genomic analysis terms into workflow phases
blocks.caption: Card sorting with subject matter experts, not a guess: the vocabulary scientists actually use.

sections.heading: Cohorts That Nest, Compare, and Save

blocks.value: Low-fidelity concepts went in front of bioinformaticians already running variant analysis by hand, and their reactions **validated the interaction model** I'd sketched: cohorts nest like folders, with parents and children, so a scientist can refine a group without losing the broader one it came from.

blocks.alt: Low-fidelity cohort-builder prototypes shown to bioinformaticians in interview sessions
blocks.caption: Tested with the bioinformaticians who'd actually run this analysis, not a stand-in audience.

blocks.value: The storyboards worked out the rest of that model before a line of code shipped: **temporary tabs** let a scientist hold several cohorts open to compare side by side, a scatter plot estimates ethnicity against 1000 Genomes Project reference data, cohort size adjusts by filtering out numerical outliers, and a finished cohort can be **saved and shared as a snapshot** rather than rebuilt from scratch by the next person who needs it.

blocks.alt: A storyboard grid walking through building a cohort, comparing multiple cohorts in tabs, estimating ethnicity, and saving a cohort snapshot
blocks.caption: The model in miniature: cohorts that nest, tabs that compare, snapshots you can hand off.

blocks.value: The Figma prototype proved the model held together end to end, dozens of connected screens, not a handful of hero shots.

blocks.alt: A Figma prototype canvas with many screens connected by blue interaction arrows
blocks.caption: Every blue line, nicknamed “noodles,” is a real connection, not a hero-screen mockup.

blocks.value: This end-to-end design was never a one-time discovery pass. I kept synthesizing **customer feedback** from scientists in the field, and one recorded call did more to shape the roadmap than most research studies. William LaFramboise of Allegheny Health Network described, almost exactly, the tool his team needed: generate a heat map of one cohort against another, light up the genes that vary, then drill into the specific mutations.

blocks.alt: A recorded customer call with William LaFramboise of Allegheny Health Network describing the need to compare gene variance across cohorts
blocks.caption: A real customer call, not hypothetical: compare gene variance across three cancer cohorts.

blocks.value: Two features shipped in response. The **Genes** tab gives a scientist fast reconnaissance on one cohort at a time, mutation types color-coded by gene, so they know where to look before committing to a comparison.

blocks.alt: The Genes tab: a mutation-type heat map by gene, color-coded by variant class, for the active cohort
blocks.caption: Fast reconnaissance on one cohort: which genes carry the most disruptive mutations.

blocks.value: **Marker Frequency** is the closer match to what LaFramboise actually described: up- and down-regulated gene percentages across several named cohorts at once, so a scientist sees which genes vary between, say, lung, prostate, uterine, and breast cases without building four separate views by hand.

blocks.alt: The Marker Frequency comparison view: up- and down-regulated gene percentages across four named cohorts at once
blocks.caption: The shipped answer: flip to Marker Frequency, compare genes across four cohorts at once.

blocks.value: User testing kept finding the smaller misses that research alone doesn't catch. Mid-session, a participant hit a real problem: rare variants were all squished to the bottom of the plot, impossible to tell apart. The fix that shipped was a single **Invert Y-axis** toggle, so rare variants aren't lost at the bottom of their own chart.

blocks.alt: A user-testing session where a participant asks to invert the y-axis so rare variants are visible
blocks.caption: “The rare variants are squished to the bottom.” The fix: an Invert Y-axis toggle.

blocks.value: The same testing surfaced an **unmet need**: scientists wanted to see the distribution of variant types per gene, and a bar chart couldn't hold six variant types cleanly. A radar chart could, one shape per gene, comparable at a glance down an entire results page.

blocks.alt: A grid of radar charts showing structural-variant type distribution per gene
blocks.caption: Six variant types don't fit a bar chart. A radar chart does, one shape per gene.

sections.heading: One System Across Three Very Different Data Types

blocks.value: Cohorts wasn't the only app I owned. I applied the same visual language and component system to **Connected Multiomics**, Illumina's proteomics and spatial transcriptomics apps, so the platform reads as one product even though the underlying science, and the charts it demands, are nothing alike.

blocks.alt: The Connected Multiomics proteomics viewer with a volcano plot and per-protein box plots
blocks.caption: Different science, same system: new chart types, same chart-beside-data-table pattern.

blocks.alt: The Connected Multiomics spatial viewer showing a tissue slice with a UMAP and transcript counts
blocks.caption: Spatial transcriptomics pushes hardest: a tissue slice and a UMAP plot, same components.

blocks.value: Every comparison view I shipped, and every session I watched, topped out at four cohorts. That was enough for the case-control comparisons customers asked for, but bioinformaticians increasingly want to line up five or six subtypes at once, and the current tabs-and-columns layout doesn't have anywhere left to grow. If I revisited this, I'd design the comparison model to scale past four before it becomes a wall of tabs.

I'd also push harder on the ethnicity-estimation scatter plot from the storyboards. It's only as fair as the reference panel behind it, and 1000 Genomes alone under-represents some of the populations these scientists study. That's a data problem more than a design one, but it's the kind of thing worth flagging rather than letting a clean scatter plot imply more confidence than the underlying data supports.

title: AI Recommendations
description: An inline recommendation model for Informatica's data-integration products, plus a precision-tracking method I convinced cross-functional teams to ship so the model keeps learning from what developers actually choose.
blurb: As Principal UX Designer, I brought AI-predicted best practices into Informatica's data-integration products, designing an inline recommendation model that suggests the next set of transformations without breaking the developer's flow. I partnered with ML engineers to shape the interaction model across cloud and desktop, and designed a lightweight precision-tracking method that I convinced cross-functional teams to ship, so the model retrains on real user choices.
team: Machine learning engineers, UX researchers, UX partners, executive leadership

hero.alt: The CLAIRE recommendations panel in the mapping canvas, each suggestion explained and one already applied to the mapping
hero.caption: Each recommendation explains why it's shown, and applies without leaving the mapping.

blocks.value: As **Principal User Experience Designer** at Informatica, I designed CLAIRE Recommendations: an AI feature that predicts and suggests the next data transformation a developer needs, trained on anonymized mapping patterns across customer tenants. I partnered with machine learning engineers and UX researchers to shape the interaction model across both the desktop client and the newer cloud product.

The recommendations only work if developers trust them and don't have to leave their flow to use them. That meant designing them to appear inline in the canvas instead of a separate list, and building a way to prove the model was actually getting better instead of just declaring it was.

sections.heading: How the Model Learns What to Recommend

blocks.value: A mapping is a data transformation workflow that moves data from a source to a target through a sequence of user-specified transformations. The model analyzes matching sequences across anonymized mappings from multiple customer tenants and, based on prior usage patterns, predicts the **“next set”** of transforms a developer is likely to add.

blocks.alt: The mapping designer shown in both the desktop client and the cloud product
blocks.caption: The same model runs in both surfaces developers use: desktop and the newer cloud product.

blocks.value: I advocated for surfacing recommendations directly in the canvas instead of a separate list to cross-reference, the way predictive text suggests the next word without asking you to open a menu. An early concept tested this literally: a recommended step rendered as a dashed placeholder right where it would go, accepted or dismissed on the spot instead of checked against a sidebar.

blocks.alt: A higher-fidelity concept rendering showing a recommended transform as a dashed placeholder directly in the mapping canvas
blocks.caption: A recommendation as a dashed placeholder in the canvas: accept or dismiss it in place.

blocks.alt: A messaging app suggesting the next words inline, used as an analogy for inline transformation recommendations
blocks.caption: The comparison that made the case: work like predictive text, not a list.

blocks.alt: The transformation menu with AI-recommended options marked by a distinct lightbulb icon
blocks.caption: One lightbulb icon set recommended transformations apart from the defaults.

sections.heading: From Napkin Sketch to Shipped Interaction

blocks.value: The inline concept above is where the idea landed, not where it started. Early sketches worked through several ways a recommendation could attach to a step: a dashed placeholder, a dropdown of ranked options, or a badge you click into. A storyboard settled the remaining details: recommendations surface as a card with a **“Show Me”** action that jumps to the step in question, can be accepted or dismissed inline, and dismissed recommendations stay reachable under their own tab instead of disappearing for good.

blocks.alt: Hand sketches exploring where and how recommendations could appear in the mapping canvas
blocks.caption: Early sketches tried several ways to attach a recommendation: placeholder, dropdown, badge.

blocks.alt: An eight-frame storyboard walking through when recommendations surface, how they are explained, and how they are accepted, dismissed, or recovered
blocks.caption: The storyboard that settled it: a “Show Me” card, accept or dismiss in place, recoverable later.

blocks.alt: An animated prototype showing a recommendation appearing and being accepted in the mapping canvas
blocks.caption: An animated prototype carried the interaction to engineering before any of it was built.

blocks.alt: Visual explorations applying Informatica's CLAIRE AI branding to the recommendations panel
blocks.caption: CLAIRE, Informatica's AI brand, applied to the shipped panel: the swirl mark and lightbulb icon.

blocks.value: My user research pointed to the **Data Integration Developer** as the primary persona. Gartner's research introduced a second: the **Citizen Developer**, a non-technical subject-matter expert who needs to build integrations without writing code. Both had to work in the same mapping canvas, part of why the recommendations couldn't afford to ask either of them to learn something new.

blocks.alt: The two target personas: the Data Integration Developer and the non-technical Citizen Developer
blocks.caption: Two personas, one canvas: the Data Integration Developer and the non-technical Citizen Developer.

sections.heading: A Precision Method Cross-Functional Teams Agreed to Ship

blocks.value: A recommendation is only worth showing if it's actually right, so I designed a simple method to measure that: track what the model predicted against what the developer actually picked, a true positive if they match, a false positive if they don't. The harder part was convincing the cross-functional teams who owned the model and the tracking pipeline to build the instrumentation for it, since it added engineering work with no visible feature to point to. Once it shipped, false positives fed back into the model so it adjusted toward what developers were actually choosing.

blocks.alt: A diagram contrasting a true-positive and a false-positive prediction, feeding user selections back to improve the model
blocks.caption: True positive: prediction matches choice. False positive: it doesn't, and retrains the model.

blocks.value: During research, one customer put the payoff plainly: “Since the last upgrade they added this function that's pretty cool.” (Keri-Ann Bowen, ETL Developer, University of Maryland)

sections.heading: Convincing Leadership to Modernize the Whole Product

blocks.value: The recommendations panel highlighted how dated the rest of the product's visual design had gotten by comparison. I worked with UX partners to redesign the look and feel, then made the case to executive leadership that modernizing the UI was worth the investment on its own, not just as a backdrop for the AI feature.

blocks.alt: The modernized visual design language applied to the mapping designer
blocks.caption: The modernized visual language I argued for: worth shipping on its own, not just a backdrop.

blocks.value: The classic toolkit didn't disappear on this project, it just carried different weight. The sketches and storyboard weren't there to document a process, they settled a real interaction question (where does a prediction live, and what happens when it's wrong) before any model output existed to design around. The artifact that mattered most wasn't a wireframe, it was the true-positive/false-positive diagram: it doubled as a spec and as the argument that got other teams to build the tracking.

What I'd revisit: the false-positive loop closes on individual choices, one developer, one mapping, but it doesn't distinguish a developer following a genuinely better approach from one working around something the recommendation got wrong. I'd want a way to separate those before trusting the retrained model as much as the first one.

title: Operational Insights
description: Built for the Monday-morning glance, not an analysis session: big numbers first, deeper analysis one click down. It shipped, and the response from users was that it finally had the right kinds of metrics.
blurb: A data-monitoring dashboard built for the quick daily glance: big actionable numbers first, deep analysis one click away. Shipped, with customers calling out "the right kinds of metrics."
team: One UX designer (Jim Reed) and one UX researcher

hero.alt: The Operational Insights dashboard: job status fast-facts above rows-processed and job-count charts and a data-volume heat map
hero.caption: Built around one idea: the Monday-morning check is a glance, not an analysis session.

blocks.value: Small teams, typically five or fewer developers and one manager, both build data-integration jobs and monitor the daily flow of data through them. I designed the monitoring experience around how those teams actually check in on their work: **the "Monday-morning check" is a glance, not an analysis session**, and treating it like one is what most dashboards get wrong.

Field observation was clear: the first look is about **large, actionable numbers**, like Rows Processed and Number of Jobs, not the pie and donut charts that fill most dashboards. I built the fast-facts row around that finding and pushed status breakdowns into a small stacked column riding along beside each number, rather than giving them a chart of their own.

blocks.alt: Hand sketches labeled Fast Facts and Insights, next to a series of higher-fidelity comps showing the same running, scheduled, succeeded, and failed counts
blocks.caption: The concept on paper before it was pixels: fast facts and insights, worked out in sketches first.

blocks.value: Those sketches carried straight through several rounds of higher-fidelity comps into what shipped.

blocks.alt: Rows Processed and Number of Jobs shown as a large value beside a small bar chart, with a hover tooltip breaking a bar into succeeded, warning, and failed counts
blocks.caption: Two fast facts, status folded into a stacked column instead of its own chart.

sections.heading: Every Fast Fact Is a Doorway

blocks.value: Every fast fact needed a next step. From a single number, a user drops into **detailed analysis views**, a filtered job list, scheduled tasks by runtime environment, without losing the thread back to where they started.

blocks.alt: The job-status fast-facts row with arrows connecting the Failed and Scheduled tiles to a filtered job list and a scheduled-tasks chart
blocks.caption: From a number to the list behind it: Failed and Scheduled tiles open their own detail views.

sections.heading: Time Series for the Second Glance

blocks.value: The second glance is analytical, not a glance at all. **Time-series charts**, a line for Rows Processed, stacked columns for Number of Jobs, correlate both against the projects and folders they belong to, over whatever date range the operator picks.

blocks.alt: An analysis screen with a multi-series line chart of rows processed by project above a stacked-column chart of job counts by day
blocks.caption: Not every question fits a fast fact: the second glance correlates rows against jobs, by project.

sections.heading: Customers Were Already Building This by Hand

blocks.value: Field visits turned up teams **piecing together their own monitoring** out of spreadsheets, ad-hoc dashboards, and a Slack channel wired to post automated status updates. I treated every one of those workarounds as a feature request already validated by the customer who built it.

blocks.alt: A collage of customer-built monitoring: ad-hoc dashboards, an email summary of processed-rows statistics, and an automated Slack channel of task-flow updates
blocks.caption: What customers built for themselves first: spreadsheets, dashboards, a Slack status channel.

sections.heading: What I Tried Based on What I Heard From Customers

blocks.value: Those workarounds were the pitch. Customers already had a Slack channel they checked all day, so instead of asking them to open another dashboard, I proposed bringing the same fast facts and anomaly alerts there. I took the idea to product management and designed a prototype: a bot, CLAIRE, that posted alerts straight into the channel and could restart a stuck agent or explain an anomaly on request, right where the team was already talking. It demoed well. It did not make the next roadmap.

blocks.alt: A Slack conversation in the Data Integration channel: teammates asking the CLAIRE bot about anomalies and to restart a stuck agent, with the bot posting a rows-processed chart in response
blocks.caption: CLAIRE, a Slack bot prototype for the same alerts and answers: demoed well, never shipped.

sections.heading: Company Logos, Not at This Scale

blocks.value: An early comp put customer logos, Salesforce, AWS, Oracle, Workday, on the Top Targets and Top Sources bar charts in place of plain text labels. Product marketing loved how it looked in the demo. I dropped it: Informatica has hundreds of connector types, many with no logo at all, and plenty of customers connect to systems that were never going to get an icon. A design that only works for the six connectors in a demo does not belong in the shipped product.

blocks.alt: Top Targets and Top Sources bar charts with company logos, Salesforce, AWS, Oracle, Workday, Azure, standing in for connector names
blocks.caption: Striking in the demo, unworkable at scale: company logos standing in for connector names.

sections.heading: Blue for Real, Green for Predicted

blocks.value: Predictive features needed a way to keep actual values from blurring together with the forecast. A plain **color code** did it: blue for what happened, green for what the model predicts. I added a "How was this prediction made?" link alongside it, so operators could interrogate the forecast instead of just trusting it.

blocks.alt: A rows-processed line chart in blue above a green shaded area chart labeled Projected Rows Processed, powered by CLAIRE
blocks.caption: Blue for what happened, green for the model's prediction, plus a way to ask how it was made.

sections.heading: What Shipped, and What Users Said

blocks.value: Post-launch, I ran feedback sessions with people using the live product. The design held up. One user put it plainly: **"I really like Operational Insights. It's got the right kinds of metrics."**

blocks.alt: A recorded customer call showing the live dashboard, captioned with the quote about it having the right kinds of metrics
blocks.caption: Nick Marty, an Informatica user, after launch: the dashboard finally had the right metrics.

blocks.value: The Slack app stayed a prototype, not a shipped feature. Customers had already proven the concept by building rougher versions of it themselves. If I revisit this work, that is the extension I would push from concept to production first.

Trust in the AI prediction mattered as much as reading it correctly. The "How was this prediction made?" link was our answer, but I never got to measure whether it actually changed how much operators trusted the forecast. That is the open question I would go back and answer.

title: Developer Experience
description: A developer portal built from scratch for GE's Predix cloud: an MVP catalog shipped fast, went in front of Gartner, and launched in full, then I moved into the PM seat myself.
blurb: A build-from-scratch developer portal and admin console for GE's Predix cloud. The MVP catalog shipped fast, got demoed to Gartner, and launched in full. I moved into the PM seat from there.
role: Senior Staff UX Interaction Designer and acting Technical Product Manager, GE Digital
team: Agile product team of developers and designers

hero.alt: The Predix Developer Network home page: an "Industrial IoT Platform" hero above a "How Predix Works" diagram
hero.caption: Three concrete starting points on the home page, not a marketing pitch: try, tutorial, app.

blocks.value: I led design (and for a stretch, product management) for a new web portal and administration console for a cloud platform's services, **built from scratch with an agile team**. The job was to get a software developer from a first visit to a running application as quickly as possible.

sections.heading: One Persona, Not a Committee of Them

blocks.value: I designed around a single persona instead of a roster of them: **Elaine the Software Architect**, cast as the main character in every storyboard. A committee of personas turns design debates abstract; one gives the team an actual person to argue about, not a feature list.

blocks.alt: A storyboard panel of Elaine browsing the Predix catalog and trying an interactive API test console against a live wind turbine
blocks.caption: Elaine's own line drove the bet: an API console against a live GE turbine, not just documentation.

sections.heading: Storyboards to Find the Critical Features

blocks.value: Product storyboards walked the full path (sign up, build, deploy, monitor) and surfaced the features that actually mattered. One target set the bar: **a base application up and running in under five minutes**.

blocks.alt: A storyboard showing Elaine's app auto-deploying to the cloud and an application dashboard where she reviews usage stats
blocks.caption: The five-minute deploy claim came from this frame, a design target, not a measured number.

blocks.value: Low-fidelity wireframes drove rapid, early iteration on the catalog and console layouts. Before any of it was built, **After Effects motion prototypes** tested how the interactions should actually behave, catching problems a static wireframe couldn't show.

blocks.alt: Wireframes of the Predix catalog of starter packs and services beside a console showing alerts, resource usage, and favorite apps
blocks.caption: The catalog wireframe led with runnable starter packs, not just a service directory to browse.

blocks.alt: A silent motion study testing hover and active-item transitions in the Predix docs navigation
blocks.caption: This behavior was proven in motion before a single line of production code existed.

blocks.value: A good UI wasn't going to be enough on its own. I pitched the marketing team on funding a series of **hands-on coding-tip videos** aimed at developers, not a generic product reel, and won the budget. I then directed the lean crew that shot them.

blocks.alt: A shot list for the developer video series: title card, medium close with lower thirds, over-the-shoulder, and screen capture shots
blocks.caption: The shot list favored over-the-shoulder and screen capture: show the code, not talk about it.

blocks.value: The videos lived on the community site, next to the developer forum and blog, where developers were already spending time.

blocks.alt: The Predix community page with forum and blog links and an embedded "A Developer's Take on Predix" video
blocks.caption: The videos sat beside the forum and blog, where developers were already looking.

blocks.value: We shipped an **MVP catalog of cloud services** quickly: eight services already live across Edge Software and Data Management alone, with Analytics and Apps categories still to come. It got demoed to analysts including Gartner, then launched in full months later.

blocks.alt: The shipped Predix catalog page, organized into Services, Analytics, and Apps tabs
blocks.caption: Eight services shipped across two categories before Analytics and Apps even launched.

blocks.value: I then moved into a product manager role myself, representing the product at GE's Minds + Machines and Industrial Internet events and carrying customer needs straight back into the roadmap.

blocks.alt: Jim Reed in conversation with a customer on the show floor at GE's Minds + Machines conference
blocks.caption: Moving into the PM seat meant working the show floor, not just designing the product.

blocks.value: The five-minute deploy target was a bet made at the storyboard stage. I never saw it checked against real usage data after launch, so I can't say whether it held up in practice. Moving into the PM seat also blurred a line I'd kept clean as a pure designer: I was now the one trading developer-experience polish against roadmap deadlines, not just arguing for it. If I did this again, I'd push for instrumentation on that five-minute number specifically, so a target set at the whiteboard could be checked against what developers actually experienced.

title: Machine Learning for Operators
description: Enabling operations engineers to train and monitor AI models without a data-science background.
blurb: Design that put machine-learning model training in the hands of the operations engineers who know the equipment best, no data scientist required.
role: Senior Staff UX Interaction Designer, GE Digital
team: Product managers and international scrum teams across California, Bangalore, and New York; UX researchers

hero.alt: An Operations Optimization dashboard with a Capacity Advisor recommendation and Digital Twin vs. actual output trends for three gas turbines

blocks.value: Training an accurate AI model normally takes a data scientist. The **operations engineers closest to industrial sensor data don't have that background**, but they understand the equipment better than anyone. This work aimed to get machine-learning techniques into their hands by reducing the complexity of the process.

With UX researchers, I ran **on-site visits** to watch the real workflow: Reliability Engineers, Data Analysts, and Data Scientists on customer floors, plus follow-up sessions sketching the model-building flow with them.

blocks.alt: A collage of site-visit photos: engineers at multi-monitor stations, whiteboard control centers, and participants sketching data curves

blocks.value: Interviews kept returning to one thing: **data exploration and curation is where the work lives**. Visualization tools let users evaluate a data set (distributions, outliers, gaps) before and after training.

blocks.alt: The AI Workbench data library: a field summary table with per-field mini distributions above a time-series chart of two sensor signals

blocks.value: The training wizard breaks the data-science process into legible steps (**Add Data, Prepare, Select Technique, Select Features, Train & Test**) with an accuracy readout and a clear path to deploy or publish a template.

blocks.alt: The Train Machine Learning Model screen: a stepper across the top, training configuration on the left, and an accuracy donut with an ROC curve on the right

blocks.value: Model output feeds **prognostic dashboards** designed for low-light industrial environments: a dark UI comparing the Digital Twin's expected output against actual readings, with a capacity optimizer recommending action.

The data-science process is iterative and perpetual because of **data drift**. Monitoring tools plot predicted against actual values and mark learning updates, so operators can see when accuracy slips and a model needs retraining.

blocks.alt: Power-output and heat-rate charts for a gas turbine overlaying actual and predicted lines, with diamond markers on re-training events

title: Mobile Emergency System
description: A next-generation 911 service that lets emergency operators, responders, and citizens collaborate during an incident.
blurb: A next-generation 911 app where operators, responders, and citizens share location, photos, and video in real time across iOS, Android, and desktop.

hero.alt: Three iPhone screens of the AtHoc app: a message list, an emergency report with a photo and map, and a map of alert zones

blocks.value: A next-generation 911 service that lets emergency dispatchers, operators, responders, and citizens share critical information (text, geolocation, photos, video) during an incident. I designed the system across **iOS, Android, and desktop**. The design goal was to make a genuinely complex system feel simple to use under stress.

sections.heading: Rapid Sketches to Find the Screen Templates

blocks.value: Early, fast sketches identified the **set of screen templates** the app would need (menu, register, emergency, message, reply, report list, send report) before any layout work began.

blocks.alt: A grid of hand sketches labeled menu, splash, register, default, slider, emergency, message, reply, report list, and send report

sections.heading: Screen Flows for the Detailed Actions

blocks.value: **Screen-flow diagrams** mapped every user action (duress, check in, report, tracking, inbox), including the operator-only paths and the branches for success with and without media.

blocks.alt: A branching flow diagram of numbered app screens covering duress, check-in, report, tracking, and inbox use cases

blocks.value: Low-fidelity wireframes carried the **early screen layout and annotation**: the emergency call button, the send-emergency-message flow, media attachments, inline location, and operator alerts with threaded replies.

blocks.alt: Annotated wireframes of a send-emergency-message screen and a message thread with operator alerts and citizen replies

sections.heading: A Mood Board for Emergency Alerting

blocks.value: Mood boards set the aesthetic direction by drawing on the **visual language of physical emergency hardware**: call boxes, pull stations, strobes. That reference informed the color palette and the skeuomorphic treatment of the emergency controls.

blocks.alt: A mood board of emergency hardware photos: SOS buttons, fire pull stations, call boxes, and red strobe lights

blocks.value: During an incident, **citizens check in with their location** and receive alerts from operators. The message list keeps a running record of check-ins, reports, tracking state, and failed sends with a retry.

blocks.alt: An AtHoc message list under a "Facility Fire" alert showing check-ins, an emergency report, and a failed report with a Retry button

blocks.value: Operators **publish map layers and pins** so first responders and civilians can track the incident, the affected area, and cordons in real time.

blocks.alt: The app map view with a shaded alert zone and two dropped pins marked NEW

blocks.value: The mobile app is one face of a larger platform. **Operators work a synchronized tablet and desktop view**, messages and the live map side by side, so field and command stay in step.

blocks.alt: The AtHoc tablet layout with a message list on the left and a full incident map with alert zone and pins on the right

title: Additive Manufacturing
description: A dashboard that turns 3D-printer sensor data into a clear productivity picture, per machine and per facility.
blurb: A monitoring dashboard that gives additive-manufacturing teams a clear Availability Score for every 3D printer and across the whole facility.
role: Senior Staff UX Interaction Designer, GE Digital

hero.alt: The Additive Console builds view: a table of print jobs by machine and site with status and progress bars

blocks.value: Customers running industrial 3D laser printers needed visibility into how their machines were operating. I designed a dashboard that gathers **sensor data** and surfaces statistical calculations, per printer and across a facility, so teams can maximize machine productivity.
Rough concept sketches illustrated the **core functionality and user value** before any pixels: an Availability Score for each machine, green or red at a glance, rolled up to the site.

blocks.alt: A hand-drawn sketch of a browser dashboard showing per-machine availability percentages, beside a smiling user

blocks.value: An early design showed the Availability Score as a **donut chart**. User testing found it confusing: the printers themselves use a similar donut to show print progress, so the metric read as something it wasn't. After concept testing it became **a number and a color indicator**.

blocks.alt: Side-by-side options labeled "donut" and "not donut": a circular progress gauge versus a large percentage with an up arrow

blocks.value: **Contextual research at a facility producing aircraft-engine parts** grounded the work: watching the manufacturing process and interviewing operators, process engineers, and reliability engineers in place.

blocks.alt: Site-visit photos of engineers reviewing production boards, standing at a control center, and operating a metal 3D printer

blocks.value: A **journey map** laid out the roles and tasks from part order to ship (design, build, finish, quality) plus the horizontal functions like fleet monitoring and operations, and flagged the MVP opportunities.

blocks.alt: A journey map with a top row of part-manufacturing steps and a lower band of horizontal functions, each tied to a role

blocks.value: Personas made the users' goals and constraints concrete. The **Operator** is "comfortable with computers, but not an expert," is responsible for loading, unloading, and monitoring builds, and above all **needs to know accurately when a part will finish**.

blocks.alt: An Operator persona card with a photo, goals, responsibilities, and a challenge about knowing when a part will be finished

blocks.value: Operators work **on call**, so the design extended to mobile concepts for checking machine status remotely: the same green/red build state, pocket-sized.

blocks.alt: A hand holding a phone showing a sketch-style "My Machines" list with green and red progress bars

blocks.value: The shipped dashboard gives each facility an **Availability Score** for every printer's productivity plus aggregate site-level metrics: the clear productivity read the operators had been missing.

title: Analytics & Big Data
description: Enterprise tools for big-data analytics on GE's Industrial Internet platform, from data exploration to analytic orchestration.
blurb: Data-exploration and orchestration tools for GE's Industrial Internet platform, giving data teams a way to see and shape their data at every step.
role: Senior Staff UX Interaction Designer, GE Digital
team: Subject-matter experts and stakeholders in collaborative design sessions

hero.alt: The Predix Insight Data Explorer: a multi-series line chart of asset temperatures above a data grid, with chart-type options

blocks.value: Research with data scientists and data engineers kept pointing at the same gap: **data exploration and cleansing is a critical part of the data-science process**, and no tool made it easy at the points in the workflow where that visibility matters most.

I conceived **Data Explorer** to give teams visualization tools for evaluating data before and after analytic processing: line, bar, and scatter views, layered assets, and the underlying data grid, all in one place.

The **Orchestration Editor** lets users catalog and sequence analytic techniques together with business logic on a BPMN-style canvas: standard and long-running analytics, gateways with explicit conditions, and a chart output.

blocks.alt: The Orchestration Editor canvas with data-object, analytic, gateway, and sub-process nodes, and a gateway-conditions panel below

blocks.value: I ran **collaborative workshops** with subject-matter experts, sketching and mapping task flows with diagrams and sticky notes. Running the sessions with stakeholders in the room gives everyone ownership of the design.

blocks.alt: A wall of sticky notes mapping a data-analysis user journey from sign-in and upload through catalog, workspace, and visualization

sections.heading: Task Flows Mapped to the Product

blocks.value: The synthesized model tied every user task to a place in the product (**Upload, Pick, Configure, Execute, Evaluate**) across Data Explorer, the Analytics Catalog, and the Analytics Workbench, with a shared Data Visualizer and a Version Tracker for iteration.

blocks.alt: A task-flow diagram with five columns from Upload to Evaluate, each grouping the detailed user actions in that product area

blocks.value: Sketches explored the **interactions and layouts**: the orchestration editor's library and canvas, dragging fields onto model inputs, the dashboard, and a dashboard designer showing multiple outputs.

blocks.alt: Hand sketches of an orchestration editor, a field-to-input drag interaction, a dashboard, and a dashboard designer
